paper_title: WorldFlow: Joint Video and 3D Motion Prediction via Large-Scale Pretraining

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Predicting future physical states stands as a central challenge in embodied intelligence. Existing video world models leave 3D dynamics implicit, action-based formulations remain tied to specific robot configurations, and 3D motion prediction models use flow-only supervision, providing a limited learning signal for physical dynamics. To circumvent these limitations, we introduce \method{}, a generative world model that jointly predicts future video and query-based 3D trajectories. By parameterizing 3D motion as continuous displacement tokens aligned with the video grid, a unified Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) backbone jointly denoises both modalities under a rectified-flow objective. This formulation couples explicit geometric dynamics with visual evolution, effectively unlocking the physical commonsense embedded within pretrained video models. To empirically scale and validate this unified architecture, we train \method{} on a heterogeneous mixture of 1.44 million object-level samples spanning simulated and real-world domains. We further introduce WorldFlowBench, comprising 1,678 evaluation samples from 11 data sources across simulated and real-world interactions, including spatial reasoning tasks. Across all three evaluation sets, WorldFlow achieves the lowest average displacement error (ADE) and final displacement error (FDE) among the evaluated learning-based methods. Notably, on the challenging SpatialCog set, WorldFlow achieves an ADE of 0.060 m, a 54.2\% reduction compared with the strongest external baseline. It also reduces ADE and FDE by 55.9\% and 68.5\%, respectively, compared with its flow-only variant. Project page: https://worldflow-rbs.github.io/.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: The philosophy of Heraclitus is often distilled into the aphorism panta rheieverything flows. In the physical world, appearances and spatial configurations continually change, while objects maintain continuity over time. An embodied world model should capture both aspects. Recent generative video models (Team Wan et al., 2025; Team Seedance et al., 2026) predict increasingly coherent visual futures, but express these predictions in pixels, leaving the underlying 3D dynamics implicit. World action models (Zhou et al., 2026; Yuan et al., 2026; NVIDIA, 2026; Ye et al., 2026) connect future prediction to robotic behavior by incorporating actions into world modeling. However, action supervision is costly to collect at scale, and action representations are often tied to particular robot embodiments, complicating cross-platform transfer. These limitations motivate extending world modeling into the space of explicit 3D motion flow: geometric representation of physical change that can connect visual prediction to planning and control across embodiments. complementary line of research approaches this space through motion modeling, progressing from tracking motion in observed videos (Lu et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2026) to predicting future trajectories from current observations (Zhang et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2026b). For generative motion prediction, producing dense 3D scene flow is computationally expensive. Existing scene-level methods instead predict motion on coarse spatial grids (Lee et al., 2026a; Li et al., 2026a). However, sparse scene flow still allocates motion tokens to task-irrelevant regions, while its reduced spatial resolution limits the fidelity of fine motion boundaries. Query-conditioned prediction offers more targeted alternative, allocating motion tokens to specified 3D locations in task-critical regions while retaining global scene context as conditioning information. Yet learning generalizable dynamics at scale faces two challenges: high-quality 3D trajectory annotations are costly to acquire, while flow-only supervision provides limited learning signal for physical dynamics, potentially limiting generalization across scenes and interactions. Jointly modeling visual evolution and explicit motion offers natural way to enrich this supervision, bringing motion prediction into generative world model. To this end, we introduce WorldFlow, generative world model that jointly predicts future video and query-conditioned 3D object trajectories through unified Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) backbone. Given an observed image, language instruction, and sparse 3D query points, WorldFlow forecasts motion at the queried locations while using the full scene as visual context. We represent trajectories as continuous tokens encoding normalized frame-to-frame 3D displacements, enriched with initial point geometry and spatiotemporally aligned with video tokens. unified rectified-flow objective jointly denoises both modalities, coupling trajectory learning with dense visual supervision of the same future. To support training at scale, we assemble heterogeneous corpus spanning simulated and real-world domains, comprising approximately 1.44 million object-level samplesequivalent to 1,224 hours of standardized 49-frame sequences at 16 FPS. We combine existing motion annotations with automated trajectory extraction, unify their representations, and apply source-specific quality control and fixed domain-level normalization for mixed-data training. We further introduce WorldFlowBench, comprising three evaluation sets, including SpatialCog for spatial reasoning in future motion prediction. On WorldFlowBench, WorldFlow achieves the lowest ADE and FDE across all three evaluation sets among non-static methods. Compared with its flow-only variant, joint video-flow generation reduces ADE by 48.5% on Sim7 and 55.9% on SpatialCog, with 68.5% reduction in FDE on SpatialCog. These results support the value of complementary visual supervision for accurate 3D motion forecasting. Our contributions are: We introduce WorldFlow, generative world model that jointly predicts video and queryconditioned 3D object motion through unified MoT backbone, combining explicit trajectory supervision with dense visual supervision. Related Work We construct heterogeneous corpus of approximately 1.44 million object-level samples from simulated and real-world data, using unified motion representations and source-specific quality control to support large-scale training. We introduce WorldFlowBench, comprising three evaluation sets including SpatialCog for spatial reasoning, and demonstrate improvements over existing motion prediction methods and videogeneration-then-tracking pipelines.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: 2.1 Predictive World Models: From Pixels to Actions fundamental objective of visual world modeling is to predict future physical states from current observations. In the visual domain, large-scale video generators establish rich appearance and motion priors to enable coherent future synthesis (Team Wan et al., 2025; Team Seedance et al., 2026), driven by architectural and training efficiencies (Huang et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025b), and extending toward physical-world prediction, interactive simulation, and semantic control (NVIDIA et al., 2025; Robbyant Team et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026; Bian et al., 2025). To bridge visual futures with robotic behavior, World Action Models (WAMs) directly incorporate the robots action space into predictive modeling, jointly forecasting future observations and actions to support end-to-end policy learning and interactive closed-loop control (Ye et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026c), while expanding toward in-context task generalization (Zhou et al., 2026), fast inference (Yuan et al., 2026), and cross-embodiment transfer (Li et al., 2026a). Paralleling these efforts, unified multimodal models integrate visual understanding with multi-modal generation (Deng et al., 2025), paving the way for comprehensive frameworks that jointly process language, pixels, and actions for physical-world modeling (NVIDIA, 2026). 2.2 3D Motion Modeling: From Tracking to Forecasting Point tracking stands as classic paradigm focused on resolving dense, pixel-level correspondences and spatial linkages over observable video sequences (Lu et al., 2026; Karhade et al., 2026; Karaev et al., 2024; 2025; Xiao et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2026). Although these trackers provide direct measurements of surface history, they operate strictly on immediate visual evidence and remain susceptible to severe error accumulation under complex occlusions or non-rigid deformations. Concurrently, predictive motion forecasting has recently emerged to offer fresh research motivations tailored for downstream embodied and robotic applications. As generative geometric interface, 3D motion flow bypasses immediate frame matching to predict future physical dynamics directly across objects and embodiments. Early work, General Flow (Yuan et al., 2024), learned languageconditioned 3D point trajectories from human RGB-D videos as transferable manipulation affordances. NovaFlow (Li et al., 2025) and Dream2Flow (Dharmarajan et al., 2025) leveraged video generation to obtain motion priors, recovering actionable 3D object flow through tracking and geometric reconstruction. Alongside these video-based pipelines, direct motion models predict future geometry without synthesizing videos. TraceGen (Lee et al., 2026a) models compact 3D traces, while PointWorld (Huang et al., 2026) predicts action-conditioned full-scene flow and ObjectForesight (Soraki et al., 2026) forecasts rigidobject pose trajectories. More recently, RoboFlow4D (Lin et al., 2026), µ0 (Lee et al., 2026b), and MolmoMotion (Zhang et al., 2026) advanced flow-guided planning, interaction-trace generation, and language-conditioned object-point forecasting, respectively. Flow representations have also become integral to policy learning and visual world modeling: LaMP (Wang et al., 2026) introduces latent 3D motion prior for action generation, EgoWAM (Li et al., 2026a) studies 3D flow as world-prediction target for human-to-robot transfer, and Hydra-0 (Li et al., 2026b) uses image-plane action flow to condition video prediction and support robot control.

sections.content: 3.1 Problem Formulation Given language instruction c, an observed RGB frame I0, and 3D query points = {p0,i}N i=1 with i=1, WorldFlow jointly predicts future RGB frames I1:T corresponding image coordinates S0 = {s0,i}N and 3D flow f1:T . All 3D positions are expressed in the initial camera coordinate system. We define flow as the frame-to-frame displacement of each query point: WorldFlow The corresponding trajectories are recovered by accumulation: ft,i = pt,i pt1,i, = 1, . . . , T. pt,i = p0,i + τ =1 fτ,i. Our objective is to model the conditional joint distribution pθ (I1:T , f1:T I0, Q, S0, c) . 3.2 Architecture (1) (2) (3) Our central design introduces 3D flow tokens as an additional generative modality for joint video-motion prediction. Built on the Cosmos-Nano framework (NVIDIA, 2026), WorldFlow retains the pretrained reasoner and extends the generator to jointly synthesize future video and 3D flow (Figure 2). The reasoner processes the language instruction, while the video VAE encodes the observed frame into clean latents. The flow tokenizer embeds noisy displacements together with initial query-point geometry and aligns their spatiotemporal positional coordinates with the video token grid (Section 3.3). Within the Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) architecture, video and flow tokens interact through full attention and attend to the reasoners causal context. At inference, future video latents and flow are initialized from noise and jointly denoised, conditioned on the clean observed-frame latents, language context, and query geometry. The VAE decodes the generated video latents into RGB frames, while the predicted flow is rescaled and accumulated to recover 3D trajectories. This joint generation process produces explicit motion alongside video without separate tracking stage. 3.3 3D Flow Tokenization We represent each query points displacement at each future frame as continuous-valued token, augmented with initial 3D geometry and spatiotemporal positional encoding. Normalization and sequence construction. To balance motion scales across domains, we normalize displacements by domain-specific scalar estimated from training data and fixed throughout training: ft,i = ft,i ad , ad > 0. (4) The normalized displacements are arranged in frame-major order, yielding three-dimensional vectors for token construction. Query point geometry encoder. We encode each query points absolute initial position and its position relative to the query-set centroid using two parallel encoders. Each applies coordinate normalization, fixed Fourier features, and an MLP. Their outputs are concatenated and fused: e3D = MLP ([Eabs(p0,i); Erel(p0,i µ)]) , (5) where Eabs and Erel denote the two encoders, and µ is the query-set centroid. The geometry embedding is shared across all future tokens of the same query point. 4 3.3 3D Flow Tokenization Figure 2. Overview of WorldFlow. These coordinates determine the rotary transformations of attention queries and keys: (cid:22) u0,i qsps (cid:18) qt rt,i = (cid:23)(cid:19) (7) (cid:23) , , , eqt,i = R(rt,i)qt,i, ekt,i = R(rt,i)kt,i. (8) The shared positional convention encodes relative spatiotemporal relationships between flow and video tokens within multimodal attention. 5 3.4 Training Objectives 3.4 Training Objectives 3.4.1 Joint flow matching We jointly train video and 3D flow generation using weighted rectified-flow objective: LFM = λvideoLvideo + λflowLflow, (9) where Lvideo and Lflow supervise vector-field prediction for video latents and normalized 3D flow, respectively. Both modalities share per-sample noise level and are jointly denoised. Losses are computed separately for each modality, excluding conditioning positions from supervision. 3.4.2 Auxiliary motion objectives To complement vector-field supervision with explicit constraints on predicted motion, we apply auxiliary objectives to clean normalized flow reconstructed from the predicted vector field. These objectives penalize frame-to-frame displacement error, cumulative displacement direction error, and relative endpoint error, encouraging both local accuracy and trajectory-level consistency. Direction errors are weighted by ground-truth displacement magnitude, while points with small net displacement are excluded from endpoint supervision. All auxiliary terms operate in normalized coordinates and use noise-dependent weighting to emphasize lower-noise samples. The complete objective is = LFM + λdirLdir + λvmagLvmag + λendLend, (10) where Ldir, Lvmag, and Lend denote the direction, displacement, and endpoint losses, respectively. Detailed formulations and derivations are provided in the supplementary material, and their contribution is evaluated through ablation experiments.

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: 4.1 Datasets We assemble heterogeneous corpus of paired videos and 3D point trajectories spanning simulated and real-world interactions. The training corpus contains approximately 1.44 million object-level samples, equivalent to 1,224 hours of standardized 49-frame sequences at 16 FPS. The data are organized into four collections: Sim7 combines seven simulation datasets: ManiSkill (Tao et al., 2024), MIKASA (Cherepanov et al., 2026), MetaWorld (Yu et al., 2020), MetaFold (Chen et al., 2025a), RLBench (James et al., 2020), RoboCasa (Nasiriany et al., 2024), and RoboTwin (Mu et al., 2025), covering diverse robotic interactions and manipulation tasks. Real3 comprises AgiBot World (Bu et al., 2025), EPIC-KITCHENS (Damen et al., 2018), and Something-Something V2 (Goyal et al., 2017), covering real-world robot and human interactions. SpatialCog is our self-collected dataset of tabletop and household interactions, with an emphasis on spatial relations in instruction-conditioned motion. MolmoMotion-1M (Zhang et al., 2026) contributes curated 3D motion annotations from six sources: EgoDex (Hoque et al., 2025), Xperience (Ropedia, 2026), YT-VIS (Yang et al., 2019), Stereo4D (Jin et al., 2025), DROID (Khazatsky et al., 2024), and MolmoSpaces (Kim et al., 2026). 6 4.2 Training Configuration and Strategy Annotation and standardization. For Sim7 and Real3, we generate captions with Gemini-2.5 Pro (Comanici et al., 2025), obtain object masks with SAM 2 (Ravi et al., 2024), and extract 3D point trajectories using Track4World (Lu et al., 2026). SpatialCog pairs manually annotated captions with Track4World trajectories. For MolmoMotion-1M, we reuse the released motion annotations, apply source-specific geometry, scale, and trajectory-validity checks, and standardize the retained sequences into 49-frame clips. All collections use shared representation consisting of video, language instruction, initial 3D query points, and frame-to-frame 3D displacements. Additional processing details and per-source statistics are provided in the supplementary material. Evaluation split. We introduce WorldFlowBench, benchmark comprising 1,678 held-out evaluation samples: 396 from Sim7, 882 from Real3, and 400 from SpatialCog. The three subsets cover simulated interactions, real-world motion, and spatial-relation reasoning, respectively. All evaluation samples are excluded from training. 4.2 Training Configuration and Strategy Implementation details. We train on 49-frame clips at 288 480 resolution with = 64 query points. The video VAE uses temporal and spatial compression factors of qt = 4 and qs = 16, followed by 2 2 latent patchification (ps = 2). Each clip therefore contains 13 9 15 video-token grid and 48 64 flow tokens. Training uses 64 NVIDIA H800 GPUs across eight nodes, with per-GPU batch size of two and no gradient accumulation, yielding global batch size of 128. Training strategy. We adopt two-stage training schedule. The first stage initializes the model from pretrained Cosmos-Nano checkpoints and trains on the SpatialCog training split for 32,000 steps. The learning rate follows linear warmup and cosine decay, with peak of 104. The resulting exponential moving average (EMA) weights initialize the second stage. The second stage trains on the heterogeneous data mixture for 51,100 steps across three curriculum phases: simulation-focused training, mixed real-world adaptation, and refinement on the SpatialCog training split. During real-world adaptation, sampling gradually shifts from MolmoMotion to Real3. Each phase prioritizes its target domain while retaining cross-domain replay, with smooth transitions between sampling distributions. After warmup, the learning rate reaches 104, transitions to an 8 105 plateau during real-world adaptation, and decays through late adaptation and final refinement. We expand task prompts into structured instructions specifying data origin, camera motion, actor type, and environment. For classifier-free guidance, text conditioning is dropped with probability 0.1, while visual and geometric conditioning is retained. At inference, we use 40 rectified-flow sampling steps with guidance scale of 2. 4.3 Flow Benchmark 4.3.1 Evaluation Metrics We evaluate 3D point trajectories in metric coordinates. Average displacement error (ADE) measures the mean Euclidean position error across query points and future frames, while final displacement error (FDE) measures the mean position error at the final frame. Both are reported in meters. PWT measures the fraction of pointframe pairs whose position error falls within given distance threshold. We report its average over thresholds of 1, 2, and 5 cm to assess trajectory accuracy at fine spatial scales. 4.3.2 Quantitative Evaluation on WorldFlowBench We evaluate all learning-based methods under single-frame protocol, where one RGB observation and language instruction are provided to forecast common future horizon without motion history. All 4.3 Flow Benchmark Figure 3. Qualitative comparison on diverse real and simulated scenes. We visualize predicted 3D query-point trajectories from µ0, MolmoMotion, and WorldFlow across SpatialCog, AgiBot, DROID, Stereo4D, Meta-World, RLBench, RoboTwin, and MetaFold. The trajectories are projected onto the corresponding input frames for visualization. predictions are converted into metric 3D point trajectories in the initial camera coordinate system. We additionally report Static reference that predicts zero flow and therefore keeps every query point at its initial position throughout the prediction horizon. We compare against two families of learned baselines. The video-generation-then-tracking family includes NovaFlow (Li et al., 2025), as well as pipelines built on Cosmos3-Nano (NVIDIA, 2026) or LingBotVideo-MoE (Robbyant Team et al., 2026), paired with Track4World (T4W) (Lu et al., 2026) or 4RC (Luo et al., 2026) for 3D tracking. The direct flow-generation family includes MolmoMotion-AR-H1 (Zhang et al., 2026), µ0 (Lee et al., 2026b), and EgoWAM (Li et al., 2026a). As shown in Table 1, WorldFlow achieves the lowest ADE and FDE among all evaluated learningbased methods on all three subsets. Relative to the strongest external learned baseline on each subset, it reduces ADE by approximately 46.9% on Sim7, 4.7% on Real3, and 54.2% on SpatialCog. It also achieves the highest PWT among learning-based methods on Sim7 and SpatialCog. On Real3, WorldFlow obtains PWT of 0.311, compared with the best value of 0.332, while still delivering the lowest ADE and FDE. These results demonstrate consistent improvements in trajectory accuracy across simulated interactions, real-world motion, and spatial-reasoning tasks. 4.3.3 Ablation Studies Flow-only versus joint generation. To evaluate the benefit of jointly modeling 3D motion and visual evolution, we compare WorldFlow with flow-only variant using the same backbone, training data, and optimization recipe. The variant predicts only 3D flow, whereas the full model jointly generates video and flow. The full model reduces ADE by 48.5%, 19.8%, and 55.9% on Sim7, Real3, and SpatialCog, respectively, with lower FDE on all three subsets. On SpatialCog, FDE decreases from 0.248 to 0.078 m, 68.5% reduction. PWT also improves on Sim7 and SpatialCog, with small decrease on Real3. These results support the value of complementary visual supervision for learning accurate 3D motion. Direct flow generation versus post-hoc tracking. To evaluate flow as an explicit generative modality, we compare directly generated trajectories with those recovered by Track4World and 4RC from videos produced by the same WorldFlow checkpoint. Direct flow generation achieves lower ADE and FDE and higher PWT than both tracking pipelines on all three subsets. On SpatialCog, it achieves an ADE of 0.060 m, compared with 0.083 for Track4World and 0.098 for 4RC. These results support incorporating explicit 3D flow into the world models generative output rather than recovering motion through separate tracking stage. Auxiliary motion supervision. We compare the full model with variant trained without auxiliary motion objectives. These objectives supervise displacement, cumulative motion direction, and trajectory endpoints through the reconstructed clean flow. Adding them improves ADE, FDE, and PWT on all three subsets, with the largest ADE reduction on Sim7, from 0.063 to 0.051 (19.0%). PWT increases from 0.527 to 0.564 on Sim7, from 0.299 to 0.311 on Real3, and from 0.436 to 0.449 on SpatialCog. These consistent improvements indicate that explicit supervision of clean motion complements the primary flow-matching objective. 4.4 Flow-Guided Robotic Manipulation Execution pipeline. We evaluate WorldFlow as an object-motion predictor within modular manipulation pipeline using 7-DoF xArm, an XHand dexterous hand, and ZED Mini RGB-D camera. Given an RGB-D observation and language instruction, we use Qwen3.8-27B (Qwen Team, 2026) to ground the target object and obtain its mask. The mask and depth image are then used to extract the target objects 3D point cloud, which provides query points for WorldFlow to predict object trajectories. T(R,O) Grasp (Fei et al., 2025) generates the initial dexterous grasp pose. Following Dream2Flow (Dharmarajan et al., 2025), local patch fitting optimizer fits locally rigid region near the grasp to the predicted object trajectories, producing an arm trajectory that moves the grasped object toward its predicted final position. Thus, WorldFlow specifies object motion, while the grasp and control modules translate it into robot execution. 9 Conclusion Group Task Caption Flow Prediction Robot Execution WorldFlow µ0 WorldFlow Pick and Place Stacking Place the watermelon doll into the small pink plate. Real-world manipulation with different flow predictors. Each task is evaluated over three trials, yielding 36 trials per method. Flow prediction and robot execution are evaluated separately for each trial. Both methods use matched initial layouts, identical grasp results, and the same trajectory optimization and execution settings; only the flow predictor changes. Bold indicates the higher success rate. Evaluation and results. We evaluate 12 tasks spanning pick and place, stacking, and relative placement, with three randomized trials per task and 36 executions per method. We evaluate flow prediction and robot execution independently. Flow prediction is considered successful if the predicted object motion is reasonable for the given instruction, while robot execution is considered successful if the full manipulation pipeline completes the task on the physical robot. We select µ0 (Lee et al., 2026b) as the baseline based on its competitive offline trajectory prediction performance among the reproducible direct flow prediction methods evaluated in our benchmark. For each paired trial, we replace only the flow predictor, keeping initial layouts, instructions, grasp results, and control settings identical. As shown in Table 2, WorldFlow achieves flow prediction success rate of 97.2% (35/36), compared with 25.0% (9/36) for µ0. Its robot execution success rate is 66.7% (24/36), compared with 11.1% (4/36) for µ0. The gap between flow prediction and execution success for WorldFlow reflects additional challenges in the manipulation pipeline, including grasp failures, trajectory optimization failures, and unstable placement during stacking. These results show that WorldFlow provides more reliable motion references and improves task completion within the shared manipulation pipeline.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented WorldFlow, world model that jointly generates future video and metric 3D flow from single observation, language instruction, and 3D query points. Continuous flow tokens are grounded in video coordinates and initial point geometry, enabling both modalities to be jointly denoised by shared rectified-flow generator. Experiments across diverse embodied domains demonstrate improved motion forecasting over direct flow predictors and video-generation-then-tracking pipelines. The current formulation requires predefined query points and inherits noise from automatically generated trajectory supervision. Future work will explore automatic query selection, multimodal futures, and joint generation of 3D flow and actions to study the benefits of explicit motion representations for policy learning. 10 References

sections.title: AI Use Statement
sections.content: We used generative AI tools to assist with translation, provide feedback on experimental methodology, and interpret experimental results. Gemini 2.5 Pro was used to generate captions for Sim7 and Real3, as described in the dataset section. We additionally used AI tools to assist with manuscript drafting, language editing, organization, and LaTeX formatting. The authors reviewed the AI-assisted content and checked technical descriptions, numerical comparisons, and conclusions against the methodology and experimental records. The authors take full responsibility for the final content of this work, including all AI-assisted text, claims, and artifacts.

sections.title: A Data Processing Details and Dataset Statistics
sections.content: A.1 Data Processing Details The main paper provides an overview of the data pipeline; here, we describe the source-specific processing details. For Sim7, Real3, and SpatialCog, we extract trajectories directly from the original videos using standardized configuration of 49 RGB frames and 64 query points per object record. Tracked pixels are back-projected using depth and camera intrinsics, and camera poses transform the resulting 3D points into the first-frame camera coordinate system. The object mask in the first frame defines the visible partial surface from which the query points are selected. RGB frames and point trajectories are generated at the same temporal indices and therefore require no subsequent temporal realignment. For MolmoMotion-1M, we reuse the released trajectories and associated geometry rather than extracting trajectories from the source videos. We transform the trajectories into the same first-frame camera coordinate system and standardize their point counts and temporal lengths. Records with fewer than eight valid object-point candidates are discarded. When more than 64 candidates are available, we use deterministic voxel-uniform sampling to maintain spatial coverage; for records with 863 candidates, we sample 64 points with replacement using fixed random seed. RGB frames and point trajectories are aligned using identical temporal indices. Intervals longer than 49 frames are uniformly subsampled, whereas intervals containing 848 frames are extended to 49 frames by repeating the final RGB frame and point positions. The resulting padded transitions have zero ground-truth displacement. The repeated RGB frames and their zero-displacement targets are included in training supervision. Quality control. In addition to format standardization, we assess trajectory quality along four dimensions: geometric validity, temporal continuity, observation completeness, and motion plausibility. Geometric checks reject invalid camera parameters, non-finite 3D coordinates, and inconsistent depthposition changes. Temporal checks detect abrupt changes in point position, depth, or object extent. Observation checks limit the fractions of trajectories that leave the image or lack valid measurements. Motion checks identify implausible displacement, velocity, and spatial-scale changes. The criteria depend on the reliability of each sources geometry and scale. For motion magnitude, SpatialCog and Real3 retain peak displacements in [0.05, 3] m, while metric MolmoMotion-1M subsets impose an upper limit of 3 m. To detect temporal discontinuities, Real3 limits the 99.5th percentile of frame-rate-normalized step displacement to 0.5 m; metric MolmoMotion-1M subsets additionally cap individual steps at 1 and speed at 15 m/s. DROID also rejects concurrent discontinuities in depth and 3D position. For spatial consistency, Real3 and metric MolmoMotion-1M subsets limit the increase in RMS spatial radius to 0.25 m. For observation completeness, these sources cap the out-of-frame fraction at 5%; metric MolmoMotion-1M subsets also cap the unobserved fraction at 5%. For YT-VIS, which lacks reliable metric scale, we instead use relative step-to-range, adjacent-depth, and spatial-radius statistics without absolute displacement or speed thresholds. Simulation records are screened for complete geometry and valid task annotations. All motion and continuity checks are evaluated before temporal padding. Figure summarizes the source-specific candidate counts and retention after formatting, quality control, and manifest validation, before the training/evaluation split. For SpatialCog, 82,831 post-prefilter candidate records yield 82,588 valid manifest records, corresponding to retention rate of 99.7%. This 16 A.2 Dataset Statistics Figure I. (b) Fraction retained after formatting, quality control, and manifest validation, before benchmark exclusion. For SpatialCog, 82,831 candidate records yield 82,588 valid records, corresponding to retention rate of 99.7%. Initial counts describe source-specific candidate pools rather than the full original datasets. Colors indicate the four collections defined in the main paper. All counts refer to object records rather than unique videos. pool includes all 400 SpatialCog evaluation samples in WorldFlowBench. These samples are excluded at training time, leaving 82,188 SpatialCog records for training. A.2 Dataset Statistics Table summarizes the processed data inventory. Real3 and SpatialCog exclude WorldFlowBench records; Sim7 uses its QC inventory before runtime exclusion. The reported 1,438,379 standardized object clips comprise 70,480,571 frame instances, or approximately 1,223.6 hours at 16 FPS. With 64 query points and 48 displacement steps per clip, they contain 92,056,256 point trajectories and 4,418,700,288 3D displacement vectors. These totals precede Sim7 runtime exclusion and may include padded frames, repeated query points, and multiple object records sharing the same source video. The MolmoMotion-1M sources exhibit substantial variation in their native temporal coverage. Figure II reports their interval lengths before conversion to the common 49-frame representation and the fraction of records requiring tail padding. To characterize the scale of the motion targets, we define the component RMS of record as mr = 1 48 64 3 48 64 t=1 i=1 !1/2 . fr,i,t2 (11) Figure III reports the distribution of mr within each source together with the source-level aggregate RMS, pEr[m2 r]. They characterize the numerical scale of the motion targets rather than physical speed or endpoint displacement.

sections.title: C Auxiliary Motion Objectives
sections.content: The auxiliary objectives supervise frame-to-frame displacement, cumulative displacement direction, and final displacement, all in normalized coordinates. C.1 Clean-Flow Reconstruction We reconstruct clean displacements from the predicted rectified-flow vector field for auxiliary supervision. Let x0 denote the noise-free displacement sequence and σ [0, 1] the noise level. Under the linear interpolation xσ = (1 σ)x0 + σϵ, the target vector field is = ϵ x0. The clean-flow estimate is bx0 = xσ σvθ. (13) The network retains its vector-field parameterization; auxiliary losses act on the reconstructed sequence. Here, x0 denotes the noise-free sequence, not the first video frame. Substituting xσ = x0 + σu into Eq. equation 13 gives bx0 x0 = σ(vθ u), and hence bx0 x0 = σ2vθ u2 . (14) Thus, squared displacement supervision is exactly noise-dependent reweighting of the vector-field squared error. C.2 Motion Supervision Let fti and bfti denote the ground-truth and reconstructed normalized displacements of point at step t. Their cumulative displacements from the initial position are dti = Pt τ =1 bfτ i. Each sequence contains = 48 displacement steps and = 64 points. We omit the batch index below for readability. τ =1 fτ and bdti = Pt Adjacent-displacement loss. The displacement loss penalizes the squared difference between predicted and ground-truth motion at each step: ℓvmag(t, i) = bfti fti2 2. (15) This loss supervises both magnitude and direction of local 3D displacements, with its relation to vector-field supervision given by Eq. equation 14. Cumulative-direction loss. Small local errors can accumulate into an incorrect overall direction. We therefore compare the directions of the cumulative displacements: ℓdir(t, i) = 1 cosε(bdti, dti). (16) Each error is weighted by the ground-truth magnitude dti2, reducing the contribution of points with little net displacement. For numerical stability, cosε computes the dot product divided by the product of the two vector norms, with each norm clamped below at ε = 106. Relative endpoint loss. To constrain the final predicted position, we measure endpoint error relative to the ground-truth net displacement: ℓend(i) = bdT dT i2 max(dT i2, δ) , δ = 0.1. (17) Only points satisfying dT i2 δ contribute. This excludes small-net-displacement trajectories, including stationary motion and motion that returns close to its starting position, for which relative endpoint error is unstable. The threshold is defined in normalized coordinates. 21 C.2 Motion Supervision Weighting and reduction. For sample b, all three objectives use the noise weight wb = 1 σb. The displacement loss averages ℓvmag over samples, steps, and points with weights wb. The direction loss averages ℓdir over the same indices with weights wbdbti2. The endpoint loss averages ℓend over eligible samplepoint pairs with weights wb. Each weighted sum is divided by its total weight plus 106; if no endpoint is eligible, its loss is zero. This weighting gives high-noise samples relatively less influence within each batch. For the squared displacement term, the coefficient on vector-field squared error before batch normalization is σ2(1 σ), by Eq. equation 14. The direction and endpoint terms impose additional trajectory-level constraints; they do not share the squared-error equivalence. Their effects are evaluated through the ablation experiments in the main paper. Training configuration. For second-stage training, the reduced losses use λdir = 0.1, λvmag = 0.1, and λend = 0.05.
